analysis.one_liner: Gives every registered voter public campaign funds to direct to candidates who swear off big donations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have given each registered voter $10–$25 per election cycle in public campaign money to direct to candidates, was referred to two House committees and died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a "Democracy Dollars" program in which every registered voter could direct public campaign funds — $10 for House races, $15 for Senate races, and $25 for presidential races per cycle — to eligible candidates. To qualify, a candidate would have to show real grassroots support (donations from 125–500 individuals, depending on the office) and agree to accept no other campaign money beyond a small startup fund and $50,000 of personal funds. The program would have been paid for by winding down the existing presidential campaign checkoff fund and transferring what was left into a new Democracy Dollars Fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered voters would get public money they could direct to candidates of their choice, anonymously, without spending their own cash. Candidates without access to wealthy donor networks could fund a campaign by demonstrating support from a modest number of small donors and then running almost entirely on publicly financed Democracy Dollars. Voters would also gain detailed electronic disclosure of how participating candidates spend the money.

how_it_helps.text: Every registered voter would get $10, $15, or $25 per cycle (House, Senate, presidential) in public funds to direct to eligible candidates or political committees, with the amount adjusted upward if private contributions outpaced program payments.

Candidates would qualify without wealthy connections by collecting qualified contributions from just 125 individuals for a House race, 250 for a Senate race, or 500 for a presidential race, alongside a modest dollar threshold — then could run on public money.

Any candidate taking Democracy Dollars would have to accept no contributions and make no expenditures beyond the program, a capped startup fund, and $50,000 of personal money — cutting the influence of large donors over participating campaigns.

Payments would be anonymous, with the administrator required to use blind trusts so candidates never learn which voters directed money to them, and all spending of program funds would be reported electronically and posted online within 24 hours.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would cover payments and administration, funded initially by terminating the presidential election campaign checkoff and transferring its remaining balance (with $63,002,400 carved out for pediatric research and the rest going to the new fund), plus annual appropriations. Candidates who opt in pay in a different way: they must give up most private contributions, which could make some competitive candidates avoid the program. Taxpayers' checkoff designation on tax returns would end.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, through a redirected public fund

drawbacks.text: The stakes per voter are small: $10–$25 is a rounding error next to what modern campaigns spend, and the bill's own adjustment formula only scales payments up to match whatever private contributions candidates raise — it does not replace big money.

The exclusivity rule cuts both ways: a candidate taking Democracy Dollars cannot accept any other contributions beyond the startup fund and $50,000 of personal money, which could deter well-funded, mainstream candidates from opting in and leave the program to candidates voters consider fringe.

The bill ends the existing presidential public financing system, including public financing of nominating conventions, and redirects the leftover balance — abolishing a program rather than layering onto it.

It creates a new five-member commission of retired judges appointed by the President, with power to impose civil penalties of up to 500% of misused funds and criminal referrals, and can take over administration in states without approved plans — a substantial new enforcement bureaucracy for an untested national program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine, if modest, expansion of political participation: small donors and non-donors would gain real purchasing power in elections, and participating candidates would be weaned off large contributions. The costs are comparatively low, since the program draws its seed money from an existing little-used checkoff fund, but the design has real weaknesses — the per-voter amounts are small, the all-or-nothing exclusivity rule could keep serious candidates out, and it replaces rather than supplements the existing presidential financing system. On balance it would likely have modestly shifted campaign influence toward ordinary voters, which is precisely what made it unattractive to move.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Ro Khanna introduced the Democracy Dollars Act on December 13, 2018, with no cosponsors.

That same day the bill was referred to the Committee on House Administration and to the Ways and Means Committee; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action of any kind afterward.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill expired in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the large-donor fundraising status quo are better off, because the campaign finance system they operate under was left completely untouched; no taxpayer money was spent either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and the big-donor status quo

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Democracy Dollars Act on December 13, 2018.

against.name: Rep. Gregg Harper
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup for the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never took up the tax provisions of the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor calendar and never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it sat in committees controlled by House Republicans until the Congress ended.

industries.industry: High-dollar campaign donors and political fundraisers
industries.note: Any candidate taking Democracy Dollars would have to refuse essentially all private contributions beyond a capped startup fund, shrinking the leverage of large donors over federal campaigns. Donors' money would still flow to candidates who stay outside the program, but the pool of reachable candidates would narrow.
Party committees could receive Democracy Dollar payments and spend them on their candidates' campaigns, giving parties a new public funding stream alongside their private fundraising.

industries.industry: Campaign consulting and political media firms
industries.note: They would keep their clients since publicly funded candidates still buy ads and services, and the bill authorizes new public outreach grants to nonprofits and local election officials; but some incumbent-facing client revenue tied to big-donor fundraising could shift toward small-dollar and publicly financed campaigns.
